title: Unveiling the antiviral inhibitory activity of ebselen and ebsulfur derivatives on SARS-CoV-2 using machine learning-bas

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper defines pIC50 = (1 / IC50 (M)), i.e. the reciprocal of IC50. The standard and universally used definition of pIC50 is the negative base-10 logarithm of IC50 in molar units (pIC50 = -log10(IC50)). Using a simple reciprocal instead of a negative log transformation is mathematically incorrect and would produce completely different (and non-standard) values, invalidating any QSAR model built on this transformed variable.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract vs. Results (MLR and ANN R² training values)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states the training-set R² values for MLR, RF, and ANN were 0.83, 0.82, and 0.92, respectively. However, in the Results section the same models are reported with R² of the training set = 0.69 for MLR ('GFA-MLR... R² of the training set = 0.69') and R² of 0.89 for the training set for ANN ('R² of 0.89 for the training set'). Only the RF value (0.82) matches between abstract and results; the MLR and ANN values are inconsistent.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract vs. Results (MLR and ANN test RMSE values)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract reports test-set RMSE values of 0.27, 0.18, and 0.09 for MLR, RF, and ANN, respectively. The Results section instead reports RMSE of the test set = 0.56 for the MLR model and RMSE of 0.05 for the test set for the ANN model. Only the RF value (0.18) is consistent; MLR (0.27 vs 0.56) and ANN (0.09 vs 0.05) values contradict each other between the abstract and body text.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 1(a) vs. text description of RF hyperparameters
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text explicitly states that four hyperparameters were varied for the RF model tuning: '(1) Max feature... (2) Min_sample_leaf... (3) Min_samples_split... (4) The number of estimators.' However, Table 1(a) lists n_estimators, Max depth, Min samples split, and Min samples leaf — substituting 'Max depth' for the described 'Max feature' and omitting any tested range for Max feature. Later the paper reports the best model uses 'a max feature of 4' even though no Max feature values were listed as tested in Table 1(a), and also cites 'a max depth of 10' which was never introduced in the four-parameter description in the text.

Table 1(a) lists 'Min samples split' values tested as 1, 2, 3. In standard Random Forest implementations (e.g., scikit-learn, implied by naming conventions like n_estimators/min_samples_split/min_samples_leaf), min_samples_split must be at least 2, since a node cannot be split with only 1 sample. A tested value of 1 is an invalid/impossible hyperparameter setting.

The text states: 'Gini importance varies between 0 and 1, with 0 representing the lowest and best possible importance. A higher Gini importance indicates greater [importance].' These two statements contradict each other: if 0 is described as both the 'lowest' and the 'best possible' importance, this conflicts with the subsequent claim that a higher value indicates greater importance (which is used later to select the most important descriptors). This conflates Gini impurity (where lower is better for splits) with Gini feature importance (where higher indicates greater predictive relevance).

The text states 'Seven ebselen analogs were tested against four strains of SARS-CoV-2 Mᵖʳᵒ.' However, the preceding Methods paragraph describes propagation and use of only a single SARS-CoV-2 strain (B.1.617.2, accession ON381169) for the live-virus efficacy assay, with no mention of four distinct viral strains or four Mpro variants being tested. This is inconsistent with the described experimental protocol.

R² is defined as R² = Σ(y_pred − ȳ)² / Σ(y_exp − ȳ)², i.e., explained sum of squares over total sum of squares, rather than the standard formula R² = 1 − Σ(y_exp − y_pred)²/Σ(y_exp − ȳ)². These two formulas are only mathematically equivalent for ordinary least-squares linear regression with an intercept fit on the same data; they are not generally equivalent for nonlinear models such as Random Forest or ANN, or when applied to held-out test data, making the reported R² values potentially invalid or inconsistent with standard definitions used elsewhere in the field.

The paper states that an external validation RMSE of 0.35 'demonstrates good predictive performance.' However, this RMSE is substantially higher (nearly 7x) than the internally reported ANN test RMSE of 0.05 and higher than the RF test RMSE of 0.18, making the characterization of 'good predictive performance' an overstatement relative to the model's previously reported accuracy.

The text states that, for the GFA-MLR model, 'R² of the training set = 0.69, RMSE of the training set = 0.16, and RMSE of the test set = 0.56, indicating that the model was predictively accurate and acceptable.' An RMSE that more than triples from training (0.16) to test (0.56) typically signals poor generalization/overfitting rather than an 'accurate and acceptable' model, making this conclusion unsupported by the reported statistics.

predicted_errors.error_location: Model evaluation statistical terms, VIF description
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'The variance inflation factor (VIF) indicates collinearity between descriptors in multiple regression models, indicating statistical significance.' VIF is a measure of multicollinearity among predictor variables and has no direct relationship to statistical significance (which is typically assessed via p-values or confidence intervals); conflating these two distinct statistical concepts is a conceptual error.
